name: Karl Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a press line at a metal stamping plant that makes brackets and seat frames for a car parts supplier. Steel coil feeds into the first press, and four presses in a row punch, bend and trim it into a bracket, about twenty a minute. I change the dies when we switch parts, watch for split metal and check parts against the gauge. There's already one robot on our line, moving parts between the last two presses, and I'm the one who resets it when it faults.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the big machines, honestly, and I like that robot more than most of the lads do. I use an AI app every day on my phone to work out fault codes and to plan die changes, and it's made me quicker. What wears me out is the pay, which is lower than the big car plants, and there's nothing else like this within forty minutes. I live with my girlfriend Ola, who works in a bakery, and we've got about three weeks saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and nothing more. At work I'd keep showing the lads how I use the app on faults. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and just learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm a bit disappointed, because I was hoping to ride the change to a better job. Without it, I'm stuck on lower pay at a plant with no competition nearby. It's fine, but it's not going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and ask the plant if I can train as a robot cell technician, because there's already one robot to learn on. I'd keep fixing and selling old power tools on the weekend, which brings in about a hundred a month. I'd try to save that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, but itchy. Like I'm parked when I want to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already like the robot on your line. What would you be doing with your spare time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be in the shed, mostly. I buy broken drills at car boot sales, fix them in my shed and sell them online, and that hundred a month is our whole savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three weeks saved. What worries you about money, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the car parts order drops, they cut overtime, and overtime is what keeps us ahead. Ola's bakery doesn't pay much either. We're fine month to month, but one bad month and we're on the credit card.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more.
I'd tell people online to **learn something** instead of waiting for government.
think: I think it's **disappointing**, because I hoped to ride the change upward.
I think I'm **stuck** on lower pay with no competing plants nearby.
do: Ask to train as a **robot cell technician**.
Keep fixing and selling **power tools** for about a hundred a month.
feel: **Calm** but itchy, like I'm parked when I want to drive.

fieldNote: Karl is the operator who **resets the robot**, which gives him an edge.

His **traditional** outlook shows in his belief in self-help over government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for anyone willing to work for it. At work I'd tell the lads to learn the robots. Online I'd say apprenticeships are the answer, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm well placed. The planning and ordering in the office move to software, and the plant buys more robots like ours. Someone has to look after them, and I want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant to put me on the robot course this year. I'd use AI every day to learn more about the robot controllers. I'd keep the tool business going, because it's a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about money if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture, where would the change hit your plant first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office first, then more robots between the presses. Every robot the stamping plant buys needs somebody to reset it, and I want to be the operator they call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about anyone else on your line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jim, who's 55 and has been on presses since he left school. He hates the robot, and he'd be the first to go. I'd try to help him, but he won't let me.

I'd say **apprenticeships** are the answer, not handouts.
think: I think I'm **well placed**, because I already reset the robot.
I think someone has to **look after** the robots, and I want that job.

Keep the **tool business** going as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and families and churches will have to step up. At work I'd say learn everything you can about the robots, fast. Online I'd say people need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's scary, because the AI could diagnose faults better than me by 2028. My hands-on job of resetting robots lasts until about 2031, then robots fix robots. I'd be 31 with skills that are fading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the robot course right away and try to be an installer, because installing them would be busy for three years. I'd grow the tool business. I'd save every bit I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the race is shorter than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028, robots by 2031. Robots that can fix robots too. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd need to be the one who installs them before that, and save hard. Three years of installing robots is a good wage, but after 2031 the robots might not need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the tool business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grow it, maybe a stall at the market, because people will still buy cheap tools. Ola and I could run it together.

I'd tell colleagues to learn about the **robots**, fast.
think: I think the **AI** could diagnose faults better than me by 2028.
I think robots fixing robots by **2031** leaves me with fading skills.
do: Get on the **robot course** and try to become an installer.
Grow the **tool business**, maybe with a market stall.
feel: **Alarmed**, like the race is shorter than I thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so get on with it. At work I'd say learn now. Online I'd share what courses are worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets me become a robot technician and earn more for a few years. I'd still be worried about the end, but I'd be better off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot course this year and look for a technician job. I'd grow the tool business and save. I'd use AI every day to stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd feel in control. It's like a die change with the clock running, you just work fast and carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. Does that give you enough room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Enough to qualify and earn, I think. Five years is enough for me to qualify as a robot technician and earn a proper wage before the robots arrive at the stamping plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about moving for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the job was right. Ola wants to stay near her family, so I'd look nearby first.

say: I'd say there's time to **get ready**.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn now** and share good courses online.
think: I think five years lets me become a **robot technician**.
I think I'd still be **worried** about the end.
do: Do the **robot course** at the stamping plant this year.
Look for a **technician job** near home once qualified.
Grow the **tool business** and save the profits.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to qualify as a robot technician and earn a proper wage before the robots arrive at the stamping plant.
fieldNote: Karl sees five years as enough to **qualify and earn** before robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to learn. At work I'd say get an apprenticeship. Online I'd say families should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. I'd have time to become a technician, maybe a team lead, and save properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot course, then aim for a team lead job. I'd keep the tool business going. I'd use AI tools more as they get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a little worry for the end. Ten years is long enough that I'd stop checking the news every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. You'd be 37. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, because I'd have time to build something. Ten years means I can become a robot technician, marry Ola (his girlfriend) and still keep my weekend tool business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still keep the tool business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, always. It's my backup, and I like it.

Aim for a **team lead** job within a few years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge with the robot disappears and I've got no savings. What would help is fast, paid apprenticeships in robot installing and a bit of help for the gap, not handouts. I'd rather learn to fix the robot than be paid to watch it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about family. My granddad worked in a steel mill, and he always said you look after your own. That's what I'd do.

portrait: Karl, 27, runs a **press line** at a stamping plant and is already the one who resets its robot.
He uses **AI every day** and runs a small tool repair business on the side.
He's **traditional**, prefers apprenticeships over handouts, and lives with his girlfriend Ola.
He's **uneasy** in most pictures but **alarmed** in AGI by 2028, when his robot edge disappears.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his edge with the robot disappears and he has no **savings**.
